subsection: 2. The role of government in supporting enterprise

notes.b: Governments support enterprise because small firms create jobs and exports, and private markets may not fund some good ideas.
points: Market failure occurs when private finance is not available for good ideas that are too risky or too small for banks to lend to.
Support helps firms grow into exporters, which brings foreign earnings into the economy.
Support for enterprise outside Dublin and the other large cities spreads jobs across regions.
Support can also encourage firms to adopt sustainable and digital practices, which benefits society as well as the firm.

notes.b: Local Enterprise Offices are the main first point of contact for small firms and are based within local authorities.
points: Local Enterprise Offices focus on micro and small firms, including start-ups and firms that want to grow.
They offer grants for start-up and expansion costs, such as equipment and technology.
They provide mentoring, training and advice on business planning, financial management and marketing.
The Trading Online Voucher scheme is a voucher scheme that helps small firms build an online presence and sell online.

notes.b: These two agencies support different kinds of firms, Irish-owned and foreign-owned.
points: Enterprise Ireland supports Irish-owned firms, particularly high-potential start-ups and firms that export or want to.
Enterprise Ireland helps firms with market research, export marketing and introductions to overseas buyers.
IDA Ireland attracts foreign direct investment, meaning investment by multinational firms that set up factories, offices or research centres in Ireland.
Foreign investment brings jobs and skills, and Irish suppliers can benefit by selling to the foreign firms that set up here.

notes.b: Finance is often the main barrier to a growing firm, and the state supports lending where banks are cautious.
points: MicroFinance Ireland provides small loans to people who cannot get a bank loan for their business, usually with mentoring attached.
The Strategic Banking Corporation of Ireland, SBCI, funds loan schemes that partner banks offer to small and medium-sized firms, which lowers the cost of borrowing.
State-backed lending reduces the risk for banks, which makes them willing to lend to firms they would otherwise refuse.
Údarás na Gaeltachta supports enterprise in Irish-speaking areas through grants, advice and property for firms that locate there.

notes.b: Tax measures reduce what firms pay or reward specific activity, but they cost the state revenue.
points: A low headline rate of corporation tax makes Ireland attractive for profitable firms and for foreign investors.
The research and development tax credit reduces tax for firms that spend money on research and development work.
Start-up tax reliefs reduce tax for new firms in their early years, easing cash flow when money is tight.
The Employment and Investment Incentive Scheme gives income tax relief to investors who buy shares in qualifying small firms, which makes equity easier to raise.
Tax measures cost the state revenue, so their value must be weighed against the activity they encourage.

notes.b: Skills and infrastructure remove barriers to growth, especially for small firms and rural firms.
points: Skillnet Ireland supports business networks that fund training for groups of firms, so small firms can access training they could not afford alone.
Education and Training Boards, ETBs, offer courses in business, technology and craft skills that firms need.
Good broadband and transport infrastructure allow rural firms to sell online and reach customers across the country.
Regional and rural supports, including grants and place-based programmes, help firms in areas with weaker markets.

notes.b: Government also sets the rules firms must follow, and those rules protect both consumers and firms.
points: Regulation sets standards such as food safety and employment rights that firms must meet, which protects consumers and workers.
Clear rules protect fair competition, so that firms with honest practices are not undercut by firms that break the law.
Government can reduce red tape, which lowers the time and cost of meeting legal requirements for small firms.
National enterprise strategy sets priorities for support over several years, which gives firms some certainty about what help is available.

notes.h: Benefits and limits of state support
notes.b: Support helps firms but has costs and limits, and its value depends on how well it targets real gaps.
points: Benefits include access to finance, advice, training and export contacts that a small firm would struggle to find alone.
A limit is dependence: firms may rely on grants and fail to build a business that survives when the support ends.
Support can favour firms that are good at applying for it, not necessarily the firms with the best ideas.
The state funds support from taxes, so schemes compete with other public spending on health and education.
Evaluation: support works best where it addresses a real gap, such as finance for exporters, rather than subsidising firms that would succeed anyway.

keyTerms.definition: A situation in which markets left alone do not supply something useful, such as finance for risky start-ups.
A local support centre, based within local authorities, that gives grants, training and advice to small firms.
The state agency that supports Irish-owned firms with high growth potential, especially those that export.
The state agency that attracts multinational firms to invest in Ireland.
Money invested by a foreign company to set up or expand operations, such as a factory or office, in another country.
A body that provides small loans, with mentoring, to people who cannot get a bank loan for their business.
A state-backed body that funds loan schemes which partner banks offer to small and medium-sized firms.
A tax relief that gives income tax relief to individuals who invest in qualifying small firms by buying their shares.

factCards.term: Three barriers that state support addresses
factCards.definition: Lack of finance, lack of skills and training, and lack of access to markets, especially overseas.

factCards.term: Services a Local Enterprise Office offers
factCards.definition: Grants for start-up and expansion costs, mentoring, training, advice on business planning, and help with online trading.

factCards.term: Enterprise Ireland compared with IDA Ireland
factCards.definition: Enterprise Ireland supports Irish-owned firms, especially exporters; IDA Ireland attracts foreign firms to set up in Ireland.
A low headline corporation tax rate, the research and development tax credit, start-up reliefs and the EIIS.

factCards.term: Benefits of state support for a small firm
factCards.definition: Access to finance, advice, training and export contacts that it could not easily afford alone.
Dependence on grants, cost to taxpayers, and benefits that go to firms skilled at applying rather than firms with the best ideas.
Sets standards for safety and employment rights, and can reduce red tape that slows small firms.
Broadband and transport infrastructure, regional grants, and Údarás na Gaeltachta in Irish-speaking areas.

questions.prompt: A small Irish firm wants to sell its products in continental Europe for the first time. Discuss how state agencies and schemes could help it.
questions.model: Enterprise Ireland can help with export strategy, market research and introductions to overseas buyers, which reduces the risk of entering a market where the firm has no contacts. A Local Enterprise Office can provide mentoring and training on business planning and export preparation, which builds the firm's skills before it spends money abroad. Access to finance is a further help, because export orders often need working capital to buy stock before payment arrives, and a state-backed loan scheme can close that gap. Tax reliefs such as the research and development tax credit can help if the firm improves its products to meet overseas standards, since this lowers the cost of innovation. Overall the support is most valuable where it addresses a specific barrier, although the firm must still make its own product and pricing decisions to succeed.

questions.prompt: Name one state agency and explain how it supports a small rural firm.
questions.model: A Local Enterprise Office gives a small rural firm local access to grants, mentoring and training that it could not easily get from a distant city. For a firm in an area with fewer customers and suppliers nearby, this support helps it plan, borrow and grow without leaving its community.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether tax reliefs or direct grants are the better way for government to support new firms.
questions.model: Direct grants are targeted, so the state can choose firms that match its priorities, such as digital start-ups or exporters, and it can see what it is paying for. However, grants need applications and administration, and they may favour firms skilled at applying. Tax reliefs apply automatically to any firm that qualifies, which reduces paperwork, but they help firms that make a taxable profit, so a loss-making start-up gets little from them. The better approach is usually a mix, since tax reliefs keep the system simple while targeted grants address specific gaps that tax cannot reach.
